e-9050.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
e-9050.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0$. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\, \rm{ m/s}$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\sin^2 x \,\rm{m/s}^2.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ what differential equation describes this motion?
e-9050.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/f187eff194f136838b67ab12b44f8f6882eafb59885a5c3f440d41492def4a42.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\sin^2 x$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
v \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = -\sin^2 x.\qquad \qquad (\ast)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(v^2) = 2v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(\ast)$ as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = -\sin^2 x.
$$

e-9051.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
e-9051.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x \,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \, \rm{m/s}^2.$ If $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x = 1 \, \textrm m.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
e-9051.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/4fdd70a4ca80965c0adce9c60be36b0712852b662cff69f9733f50c739fd1b32.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

e-9455.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
e-9455.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\textrm m,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
e-9455.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/eca36626e6a0cfb30d293e684483c37ddce6f18d4004c3f77258e9663565d8d7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = \dfrac{3C_1}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/2} =3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{2/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and the magnitude of its acceleration is 6x3m/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
dvdx=−6x3
b
dvdx=6x3
c
ddx(12v2)=6x3
d
ddx(12v2)=−6x3
e
ddx(v2)=−6x3
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x>0, acceleration toward the origin is negative: dv/dt=-6x^3. The chain rule gives dv/dt=v(dv/dx)=d(v^2/2)/dx, so option d describes the motion.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Question 1
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and the magnitude of its acceleration is 6x3m/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
dvdx=−6x3
b
dvdx=6x3
c
ddx(12v2)=6x3
d
ddx(12v2)=−6x3
e
ddx(v2)=−6x3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P has magnitude 6x3 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−6x3.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=−6x3.

Now, since v=dxdt, we have vdvdx=6x3.(∗)

Finally, using the fact that

ddx(v2)=2vdvdx⟹ddx(12v2)=vdvdx,

we can write our differential equation (∗) as

ddx(12v2)=−6x3.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/52fc197612dac35373ecebf771b8444505902b5c6e00c7c55d2b21dab4809136.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is x2+3m/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
ddx(2v2)=−x2+3
b
ddx(12v2)=−x2+3
c
ddx(12v2)=x2+3
d
dvdx=x2+3
e
dvdx=−x2+3
Submit

decision.explanation: For x>0, acceleration toward O is negative, so dv/dt=-√(x²+3). By the chain rule, dv/dt=v(dv/dx)=d(v²/2)/dx. Thus option b describes the motion.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/00da8cdff7814df7368ff00924360db24a93934c5ae1c87ceb5daa6b00df37a7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

Question 2
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is x2+3m/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
ddx(2v2)=−x2+3
b
ddx(12v2)=−x2+3
c
ddx(12v2)=x2+3
d
dvdx=x2+3
e
dvdx=−x2+3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is x2+3 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−x2+3.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=−x2+3.

Now, since v=dxdt, we have vdvdx=−x2+3.(∗)

Finally, using the fact that ddx(v2)=2vdvdx⟹ddx(12v2)=vdvdx,

we can write our differential equation (∗) as ddx(12v2)=−x2+3.

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution explicitly gives option b. This agrees with the chain rule: d(v²/2)/dx=v(dv/dx)=dv/dt=-√(x²+3). The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/00da8cdff7814df7368ff00924360db24a93934c5ae1c87ceb5daa6b00df37a7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

Question 3
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 2xm/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
ddx(12v2)=2x
b
ddx(12v2)=−2x
c
dvdx=2x
d
ddx(v2)=−2x
e
dvdx=−2x
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x>0, acceleration toward the origin gives dv/dt=-2^x. By the chain rule, dv/dt=v(dv/dx)=d(v²/2)/dx, so the correct equation is option b.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{2}^{x}.
$$

Question 3
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 2xm/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
ddx(12v2)=2x
b
ddx(12v2)=−2x
c
dvdx=2x
d
ddx(v2)=−2x
e
dvdx=−2x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 2x and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−2x.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=−2x.

Now, since v=dxdt, we have vdvdx=−2x.(∗)

Finally, using the fact that

ddx(v2)=2vdvdx⟹ddx(12v2)=vdvdx,

we can write our differential equation (∗) as

ddx(12v2)=−2x.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${2}^{x}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/b69783c5b926cb22a6e4321b449d006071917618da601d0ba2bfa109ffde6a0f.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${2}^{x}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{2}^{x}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{2}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-{2}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{2}^{x}.
$$

Question 4
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 4x2m/s2. Which differential equation describes this motion?

a
v2dvdx=4x2
b
 vdvdx=4x2
c
1vdvdx=4x2
d
dvdx=4x2
e
12v2dvdx=4x2
Submit

decision.explanation: By the chain rule, acceleration is dv/dt=(dv/dx)(dx/dt)=v(dv/dx). Setting this equal to 4x² gives option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/888a2f1f537f7381379a6f85dc850f29b42193eb53938832be8ede47fbe8264a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Question 4

A particle P moves along the x-axis. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 4x2m/s2. Which differential equation describes this motion?

a
v2dvdx=4x2
b
 vdvdx=4x2
c
1vdvdx=4x2
d
dvdx=4x2
e
12v2dvdx=4x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 4x2m/s2, we have dvdt=4x2.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=4x2.

Now, since v=dxdt, we obtain the differential equation vdvdx=4x2.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution states v(dv/dx)=4x², exactly option b. This follows from dv/dt=(dv/dx)(dx/dt) and dx/dt=v. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/888a2f1f537f7381379a6f85dc850f29b42193eb53938832be8ede47fbe8264a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 3x2+1m/s2. Which differential equation describes this motion?

a
2v2dvdx=3x2+1
b
2dvdx=3x2+1
c
dvdx=3x2+1
d
12vdvdx=3x2+1
e
vdvdx=3x2+1
Submit

decision.explanation: The chain rule gives acceleration dv/dt=(dv/dx)(dx/dt)=v(dv/dx). Equating this to 3/(x²+1) gives option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\text{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/f03ad90557b4bf978ece899892cada200873e920c8e00a0c196728108fee55c4.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Question 5
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 3x2+1m/s2. Which differential equation describes this motion?

a
2v2dvdx=3x2+1
b
2dvdx=3x2+1
c
dvdx=3x2+1
d
12vdvdx=3x2+1
e
vdvdx=3x2+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 3x2+1m/s2, we have dvdt=3x2+1.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=3x2+1.

Now, since v=dxdt, we obtain the differential equation vdvdx=3x2+1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\text{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/f03ad90557b4bf978ece899892cada200873e920c8e00a0c196728108fee55c4.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

before.name: Question 6
before.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 4(1+2x)m/s2. If P has a displacement of 1m when its velocity is −4m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=−(2+x+x2)
b
v(x)=−2(x+x2)
c
v(x)=−23x+x2
d
v(x)=−2(3x+5x2)
e
v(x)=−22(x+x2)
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating v(dv/dx)=4(1+2x) gives v²/2=4x+4x²+C. Using v(1)=-4 gives C=0, hence v²=8(x+x²). Motion in decreasing x requires the negative root, giving option e.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/466c0aa389beb6d1a42092b73bae75508ef2c50f1f08cca5efaac20d25615f30.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4(1+2x).
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4(1+2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4(1+2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4(x+{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=-4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-4)^{2} & =4(1+{1}^{2})+C \\ 8 & =8+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+0 \\ {v}^{2} & =8(x+{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.
$$

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 4(1+2x)m/s2. If P has a displacement of 1m when its velocity is −4m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=−(2+x+x2)
b
v(x)=−2(x+x2)
c
v(x)=−23x+x2
d
v(x)=−2(3x+5x2)
e
v(x)=−22(x+x2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 4(1+2x)m/s2, we have dvdt=4(1+2x).

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as ddx(12v2)=4(1+2x).

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫4(1+2x)dx which gives the general solution 12v2=4(x+x2)+C.

Now, since x=1m when v=−4m/s, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12v2=4(x+x2)+C12(−4)2=4(1+12)+C8=8+CC=0

Therefore, 12v2=4(x+x2)+0v2=8(x+x2)v=±22(x+x2).

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing x, we have that v(x)<0, so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore, v(x)=−22(x+x2).

before.html:
Question 7
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 116xm/s2. If P has a displacement of 0m when its velocity is −2m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=1216−x2
b
v(x)=−12x2+16
c
v(x)=−x2+4
d
v(x)=−14x2+64
e
v(x)=1464−x2
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating v(dv/dx)=x/16 gives v²=x²/16+C. The condition v(0)=-2 gives C=4. Taking the negative root for decreasing x yields v(x)=-(1/4)√(x²+64), option d; the condition at zero sets the boundary value.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$

Question 7
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 116xm/s2. If P has a displacement of 0m when its velocity is −2m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=1216−x2
b
v(x)=−12x2+16
c
v(x)=−x2+4
d
v(x)=−14x2+64
e
v(x)=1464−x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 116xm/s2, we have

dvdt=116x.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as ddx(12v2)=116x.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(116x)dx which gives the general solution 12v2=132x2+C.

Now, since x=0m when v=−2m/s, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12v2=132x2+C12(−2)2=132(0)2+C2=0+CC=2

Therefore, 12v2=132x2+2v2=116x2+4v2=116(x2+64)v=±14x2+64.

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing x, we have that v(x)<0, so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore, v(x)=−14x2+64.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution explicitly concludes v(x)=-(1/4)√(x²+64), matching option d. Integrating gives v²=x²/16+4, and decreasing x requires the negative root. The incorrect feedback concerns deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$

Question 8
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from O is xm, its velocity is vm/s, the magnitude of its acceleration is 2x2+1m/s2 and the acceleration is directed toward O. If v=−πm/s when x=1m, find the velocity of P when x=3m. Round your answer to one decimal place.

a
−1.1m/s
b
−3.1m/s
c
−1.7m/s
d
−2.6m/s
e
−0.9m/s
Submit

decision.explanation: Acceleration toward O gives v(dv/dx)=-2/(x²+1). Integrating yields v²/2=-2 arctan(x)+C. Using v(1)=-√π gives C=π, so v(3)=-√(2π-4 arctan(3))≈-1.1345 m/s, which rounds to -1.1 m/s.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/3278eca2ae91f59c7c20d91f9190611291924dcc0cd6ffe74456552ba8400335.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ {v}^{2} & =2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡3)} \\  & ≈-1.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Question 8
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from O is xm, its velocity is vm/s, the magnitude of its acceleration is 2x2+1m/s2 and the acceleration is directed toward O. If v=−πm/s when x=1m, find the velocity of P when x=3m. Round your answer to one decimal place.

a
−1.1m/s
b
−3.1m/s
c
−1.7m/s
d
−2.6m/s
e
−0.9m/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle P is 2x2+1m/s2 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−2x2+1.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2) we can rewrite our equation as ddx(12v2)=−2x2+1. Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(−2x2+1)dx which gives the general solution 12v2=−2arctan⁡x+C.

Now, since v=−πm/s when x=1m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12(−π)2=−2arctan⁡1+Cπ2=−2⋅π4+CC=π

Therefore, 12v2=π−2arctan⁡xv2=2(π−2arctan⁡x)v=±2(π−2arctan⁡x).

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing x, we have that v(x)<0, so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore, v=−2(π−2arctan⁡x).

Finally, the velocity of P at x=3 is given by v=−2(π−2arctan⁡3)≈−1.1m/s, rounded to one decimal place.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/3278eca2ae91f59c7c20d91f9190611291924dcc0cd6ffe74456552ba8400335.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ {v}^{2} & =2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡3)} \\  & ≈-1.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Question 9

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is ex−3m/s2. If P has a displacement of 3m when its velocity is 2m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=2(ex−3+1)
b
v(x)=3ex−3−1
c
v(x)=ex−3+1
d
v(x)=3ex−3+1
e
v(x)=ex−3+3
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating v(dv/dx)=e^(x-3) gives v²/2=e^(x-3)+C. Using v(3)=2 gives C=1. Since x is increasing, take the positive root: v(x)=√(2(e^(x-3)+1)), option a.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $3\,m$ when its velocity is $2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/164c90893a07ae9657e90b6f2b25e53c9c4927b1f4a076429ba0521a98377f24.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {e}^{x-3}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={e}^{x-3}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=3\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & ={e}^{3-3}+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({e}^{x-3}+1) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.
$$

Question 9

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is ex−3m/s2. If P has a displacement of 3m when its velocity is 2m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=2(ex−3+1)
b
v(x)=3ex−3−1
c
v(x)=ex−3+1
d
v(x)=3ex−3+1
e
v(x)=ex−3+3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is ex−3m/s2, we have dvdt=ex−3.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as ddx(12v2)=ex−3.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫ex−3dx which gives the general solution

12v2=ex−3+C.

Now, since x=3m when v=2m/s, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12v2=ex−3+C12(2)2=e3−3+C2=1+CC=1

Therefore, 12v2=ex−3+1v2=2(ex−3+1)v=±2(ex−3+1).

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore, v(x)=2(ex−3+1).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares v(x)=√(2(e^(x−3)+1)), exactly option a. Integrating v(dv/dx)=e^(x−3) and applying v(3)=2 confirms this result, with the positive root required for increasing x. The incorrect feedback concerns deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $3\,m$ when its velocity is $2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/164c90893a07ae9657e90b6f2b25e53c9c4927b1f4a076429ba0521a98377f24.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {e}^{x-3}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={e}^{x-3}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=3\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & ={e}^{3-3}+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({e}^{x-3}+1) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.
$$

Question 10

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x, away from a fixed origin O. When the displacement of P from O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is (2+3e−x)m/s2. If v=2m/s when x=0m, find the velocity of P when x=3m. Round your answer to one decimal place.

a
 4.7 m/s
b
 5.1 m/s
c
 3.8 m/s
d
 3.4 m/s
e
 4.2 m/s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating v(dv/dx)=2+3e^(-x) gives v²/2=2x−3e^(-x)+C. Using v(0)=2 gives C=5. Thus v(3)=√(22−6e^(-3))≈4.658 m/s, which rounds to 4.7 m/s; take the positive root because x is increasing.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Question 10
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x, away from a fixed origin O. When the displacement of P from O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is (2+3e−x)m/s2. If v=2m/s when x=0m, find the velocity of P when x=3m. Round your answer to one decimal place.

a
 4.7 m/s
b
 5.1 m/s
c
 3.8 m/s
d
 3.4 m/s
e
 4.2 m/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is (2+3e−x)m/s2, we have dvdt=2+3e−x.

Using the fact that

dvdt=ddx(12v2)

we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=2+3e−x.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have

∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(2+3e−x)dx

which gives the general solution

12v2=2x−3e−x+C.

Now, since v=2m/s when x=0m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows:

12(2)2=2(0)−3e−0+C2=−3+CC=2+3C=5

Therefore,

12v2=2x−3e−x+5v2=4x−6e−x+10v=±4x−6e−x+10.

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore, v=4x−6e−x+10.

Finally, the velocity of P at x=3 is given by v=4(3)−6e−3+10v=22−6e−3v≈4.7m/s, rounded to one decimal place.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.
